analysis.one_liner: Freezes credit card interest rates and fees on existing balances for nine months.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred credit card issuers from raising interest rates, fees, or finance charges on balances people already owed for a nine-month window, ending in February 2010. It would have closed the gap between the May 2009 CARD Act, which limited future rate hikes, and its February 2010 effective date, a period when issuers could still raise rates on existing balances. The Federal Reserve could write rules to enforce it. The bill got only three cosponsors and never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Households carrying credit card debt. By freezing rates and fees on outstanding balances for nine months, the bill would have stopped issuers from raising the price of money already borrowed, at a time when the CARD Act's protections had not yet taken effect. Because the freeze took effect immediately upon enactment, with no waiting period for rules, existing balances would have been locked in right away.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any creditor from increasing the APR, fee, or finance charge applicable to an outstanding balance on any credit card account during the nine-month period.
Prohibits creditors from changing the terms governing repayment of outstanding balances during that period, except as already allowed under the CARD Act's amendments to the Truth in Lending Act.
Takes effect immediately upon enactment, regardless of whether the Federal Reserve has issued implementing rules, so the freeze would apply to existing balances without a waiting period.

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers, which would lose the ability to raise rates and fees on balances cardholders already owed during the freeze period. Issuers had been repricing existing balances ahead of the CARD Act's February 2010 effective date; the bill would have halted that for nine months, and issuers could respond by tightening new lending.

drawbacks.text: The freeze is temporary — nine months — rather than a permanent cap, so it would only postpone rate increases until the freeze expires, after which issuers could raise rates within CARD Act rules.

Lenders price card interest to reflect the risk that borrowers will not repay; freezing rates on existing balances limits issuers' ability to reprice that risk, and issuers argued such controls lead them to tighten credit availability and raise rates on new lending to compensate.
The bill leaves cardholders' existing balances in place and does not reduce principal; it only prevents the price of that debt from rising during the window.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For families carrying card balances through the 2009 recession and slow recovery, the bill would have delivered a real, immediate benefit: nine months of a locked rate and unchanged repayment terms on money already borrowed, at a moment when issuers could still legally raise rates before the CARD Act took effect in February 2010. The main honest objection is that it is a temporary bridge, not a permanent cap, and it shifts some cost to issuers who could tighten new credit in response. On balance, the protection it offered borrowers was concrete but narrow in scope and duration.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so the full House never voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Betsy Markey of Colorado introduced the Credit Card Rate Freeze Act of 2009 on October 28, 2009, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day.

The bill would have imposed a nine-month moratorium on increases to APRs, fees, or finance charges on outstanding credit card balances, and on changes to repayment terms, running until nine months after the CARD Act's enactment.
The freeze took effect immediately upon enactment, regardless of whether the Federal Reserve had issued regulations, so protection for existing balances would not have waited on rulemaking.
No further action is recorded after the referral: the committee never scheduled a markup, and no vote was ever held in the House or Senate before the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

The bill's window of relevance was time-limited by design — the freeze would have ended in February 2010, when the CARD Act's own protections against rate increases on existing balances took effect — and the bill died before that date arrived.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers were better off because the bill never advanced: they retained the ability to raise rates and fees on existing balances during the period before the CARD Act's protections took effect in February 2010. Borrowers carrying card debt got no relief from this bill, though the CARD Act itself, already law, did eventually restrict rate increases on existing balances.

for.name: Rep. Betsy Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on October 28, 2009 to freeze credit card rates and fees on outstanding balances for nine months.

for.name: 3 of 253 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only recorded support beyond the sponsor.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on October 28, 2009 and took no further action — no markup, no report — leaving it without a House vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the party split on the bill was never tested; its three cosponsors were all Democrats, but with only four total supporters the low cosponsor count, not a floor vote, is the main signal.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and consumer banks
industries.note: The bill would have barred issuers from raising APRs, fees, and finance charges on balances cardholders already owed during a nine-month window ending February 2010 — the period between the CARD Act's passage and its effective date when issuers could still reprice existing debt. Issuers' gain came from charging borrowers more on money already borrowed, so their interest ran against cardholders in this bill.
